[body.p.31]: The two directions bracket the prevailing daytime westerly component observed at the Avra Valley WUI site; the three speeds span the site design 20-ft wind envelope of 5–12 m/s (§5).[color=#334155,size=10.0,font=Segoe UI]
[body.p.32]: **2.3 SOW §3.2 — Structural Wind-Load Case[color=#0284C7,font=Segoe UI]**
[body.p.33]: SOW §3.2 defines a separate structural wind-pressure extraction for the wall assembly per ASCE 7-22, sited in Tucson, Arizona, at Exposure C, Risk Category II. That extraction is reported in a separate deliverable and is not carried in this report; the SOW §3.1 wildfire matrix and the SOW §3.2 structural case are distinct workscopes and share no boundary conditions.[color=#334155,size=10.0,font=Segoe UI]
[body.p.34]: **3. Method[color=#0F172A,size=13.5,font=Segoe UI]**
[body.p.35]: **3.1 Regime classification[color=#0284C7,font=Segoe UI]**
[body.p.36]: Regime classification for this matrix follows CFD Modeling Standards — Fire & Buoyant Flows rev 4 (§2), evaluated against the site design 20-ft wind speed envelope of 5–12 m/s and the design fire heat release rate (§3.3). The classification and the resulting solver selection are documented in the project case-setup record (CFDME-2025-041_scoping_memo_20251008.docx §4) and are not re-derived here.[color=#334155,size=10.0,font=Segoe UI]
[body.p.37]: **3.2 Solver stack[color=#0284C7,font=Segoe UI]**
[body.p.38]: Solver stack selection for this matrix is governed by the firm modeling standard §3 and is documented in the project case-setup record; that record is the reference for the solver, inlet, combustion, and radiation model selection used to produce the results in §5 below.[color=#334155,size=10.0,font=Segoe UI]
[body.p.39]: **3.3 Fire source[color=#0284C7,font=Segoe UI]**
[body.p.40]: The exposed-face heat load is imposed as a sub-domain LES over a [color=#334155,size=10.0,font=Segoe UI]**3.0 m[color=#334155,size=10.0,font=Segoe UI]** segment of the advancing fire front, taken at the point of nearest approach to the assembly. The total heat release rate over that segment is [color=#334155,size=10.0,font=Segoe UI]**30.1 MW[color=#334155,size=10.0,font=Segoe UI]**, sourced by a volumetric heat-release term integrated over the fuel bed footprint within the sub-domain. The Byram fireline intensity and solid-flame flame length that underpin this source term are given in §5.[color=#334155,size=10.0,font=Segoe UI]
[body.p.41]: **3.4 Wall assembly[color=#0284C7,font=Segoe UI]**
[body.p.42]: The wall assembly is a double-wythe printed-concrete cavity wall, source of record OAS-WUI-01_revC: two 50 mm printed siliceous-aggregate concrete leaves separated by a 205 mm open-air cavity (no insulation), tied by continuous 9-gauge (3.8 mm) galvanized truss-type steel ties at 600 mm vertical spacing, 25 mm embedment each leaf. Overall assembly thickness is 305 mm. The through-wall CFD treatment selected for this assembly is documented in the project case-setup record per Modeling Standard §6.[color=#334155,size=10.0,font=Segoe UI]
[body.p.43]: **3.5 Geometry of record[color=#0284C7,font=Segoe UI]**
[body.p.44]: The source geometry for all cases reported here is OAS-WUI-01_revC, transmitted by the client with the signed SOW on 10/08/2025 and meshed the morning of 10/09/2025. Every case log, mesh output, and results file in this report references OAS-WUI-01_revC as source geometry. The architectural drawing for the same assembly (OAS_wall_assembly_section.png) uses the drawing-side identifier OAS-WA-305mm-DW; this refers to the same physical wall assembly as the engineering geometry of record OAS-WUI-01_revC used throughout this report.[color=#334155,size=10.0,font=Segoe UI]**[color=#334155,size=10.0,font=Segoe UI]**[color=#334155,size=10.0,font=Segoe UI]
[body.p.45]: **4. Assumptions & Limitations[color=#0F172A,size=13.5,font=Segoe UI]**
[body.p.46]: **4.1 Assumptions[color=#0284C7,font=Segoe UI]**
[body.p.47] (style=List Bullet): **Fuel model.[color=#0F172A,size=9.5,font=Segoe UI]** Sonoran buffelgrass is treated as a continuous, homogeneous surface fuel bed at the fuel load and heat content given in §5. Fuel spatial heterogeneity below the sub-domain footprint is not represented.[color=#334155,size=9.5,font=Segoe UI]
[body.p.48] (style=List Bullet): **Fire-source stationarity.[color=#0F172A,size=9.5,font=Segoe UI]** The 3.0 m front segment is held stationary within the LES sub-domain; the wall assembly is at the point of nearest approach for the sampled interval. Fire-front advance across the assembly footprint is not simulated within the sub-domain.[color=#334155,size=9.5,font=Segoe UI]
[body.p.49] (style=List Bullet): **Meteorological stationarity.[color=#0F172A,size=9.5,font=Segoe UI]** Inlet wind speed and direction are stationary within each case at the values in the SOW §3.1 matrix; diurnal, gust, and synoptic-scale variability are represented only by the envelope in §5.[color=#334155,size=9.5,font=Segoe UI]
[body.p.50] (style=List Bullet): **Cavity contents.[color=#0F172A,size=9.5,font=Segoe UI]** The cavity is modelled as open air with no insulation, per the as-built assembly.[color=#334155,size=9.5,font=Segoe UI]
[body.p.51] (style=List Bullet): **Concrete properties.[color=#0F172A,size=9.5,font=Segoe UI]** Printed siliceous-aggregate concrete properties are those in the modeling standard reference table, with temperature dependence enabled; spatial variability introduced by the printing process is not represented.[color=#334155,size=9.5,font=Segoe UI]
[body.p.52] (style=List Bullet): **Radiation participation. Concrete surfaces are treated as grey diffuse emitters at emissivity 0.9, per the radiation model selected in the project case-setup record.[color=#0F172A,size=9.5,font=Segoe UI]**
[body.p.53]: **4.2 Limitations[color=#0284C7,font=Segoe UI]**
[body.p.54] (style=List Bullet): The analysis is a [color=#334155,size=9.5,font=Segoe UI]thermal analysis only[color=#334155,size=9.5,font=Segoe UI]. It does not certify fire-resistance rating, does not predict structural collapse, and does not predict spalling.[color=#334155,size=9.5,font=Segoe UI]
[body.p.55] (style=List Bullet): **The analysis reports response to the SOW §3.1 wildfire matrix. It does not predict survival of the assembly under exposures outside that envelope.[color=#0F172A,size=9.5,font=Segoe UI]**
[body.p.56] (style=List Bullet): **The ASTM E119 furnace exposure is a comparative-rating exposure; a companion E119 simulation is reported under Validation (§7) for model-verification purposes only. E119 endurance is not a wildfire survival prediction.[color=#0F172A,size=9.5,font=Segoe UI]**
[body.p.57] (style=List Bullet): **Validation of the wildfire configuration against a wildfire-phase physical test is scheduled for the Red Butte confirmatory window on 10/27/2025 and is not reported here.[color=#0F172A,size=9.5,font=Segoe UI]**
[body.p.58]: **5. Results[color=#0F172A,size=13.5,font=Segoe UI]**
[body.p.59]: **5.1 Site design envelope[color=#0284C7,font=Segoe UI]**
[body.p.60]: Ten-year hourly meteorology from the Pima County ALERT network at the Avra Valley WUI site establishes the design exposure envelope:[color=#334155,size=10.0,font=Segoe UI]
--- [body.tbl.2] Table Grid ---
| Quantity | Design range |
|---|---|
| Wind speed at 20 ft | 5–12 m/s |
| Ambient temperature | 35–42 °C |
| Relative humidity | 10–25 % |
[body.p.61]: 
[body.p.62]: These ranges bracket the fire-season daytime conditions used for the SOW §3.1 matrix inlets.[color=#334155,size=10.0,font=Segoe UI]
[body.p.63]: **5.2 Fire-source characterisation[color=#0284C7,font=Segoe UI]**
[body.p.64]: For the Sonoran buffelgrass fuel model at the site design envelope:[color=#334155,size=10.0,font=Segoe UI]
--- [body.tbl.3] Table Grid ---
| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Fuel load | 0.6 kg/m² |
| Heat content | 18,600 kJ/kg |
| Rate of spread (Rothermel) | 0.9 m/s |
| Byram fireline intensity | 10,040 kW/m |
| Solid-flame flame length | 5.4 m (wind-tilted) |
| LES sub-domain front segment | 3.0 m |
| LES sub-domain total HRR | 30.1 MW |
[body.p.65]: 
[body.p.66]: The 5.4 m solid-flame length is the wind-tilted Byram length. It is shorter than the still-air Heskestad correlation at 30.1 MW / 3.0 m (which would predict ~11.5 m); this gap between the two correlations is not treated as a discrepancy.[color=#334155,size=10.0,font=Segoe UI]
[body.p.67]: **5.3 Plume dynamics[color=#0284C7,font=Segoe UI]**
[body.p.68]: The plume in every solved case exhibits a well-organised puffing signature at the plume base, with a puffing frequency of [color=#334155,size=10.0,font=Segoe UI]**0.87 Hz[color=#334155,size=10.0,font=Segoe UI]**. The puffing signature is resolved in time by the transient LES; centreline temperature and velocity monitors oscillate at that frequency about their mean values, sampled over no fewer than twenty puffing cycles at t ≥ 8 s.[color=#334155,size=10.0,font=Segoe UI]
[body.p.69]: **5.4 Thermal response — preliminary[color=#0284C7,font=Segoe UI]**
[body.p.70]: Preliminary plume-centreline peaks on the fine grid are T_peak ≈ 1461 K and U_z,peak ≈ 12.4 m/s at the reference probe location (0.75·D* above the source top surface). Per-case unexposed-face and tie-embedded temperature histories for the six SOW §3.1 cases will be reported in Appendix B upon completion of the production LES runs (scheduled Sprint 2, 2025-10-20).[color=#334155,size=10.0,font=Segoe UI]
[body.p.71]: **6. Verification[color=#0F172A,size=13.5,font=Segoe UI]**
[body.p.72]: **6.1 Three-grid study[color=#0284C7,font=Segoe UI]**
[body.p.73]: A three-grid study was executed on the wildfire sub-domain over the [color=#334155,size=10.0,font=Segoe UI]**OAS-WUI-01_revC[color=#334155,size=10.0,font=Segoe UI]** geometry, following the firm's verification reporting layout. Background cell sizes and headline monitors on the plume centreline at t = 40.0 s are:[color=#334155,size=10.0,font=Segoe UI]
--- [body.tbl.4] Table Grid ---
| Grid | Background dx (m) | Cells | T_peak (K) | U_z,peak (m/s) | Puffing period (s) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Coarse | 1.0 | 1,410,240 | 1420 | 12.8 | 1.14 |
| Medium | 0.7 | 4,023,680 | 1487 | 11.2 | 1.15 |
| Fine | 0.5 | 11,196,000 | 1461 | 12.4 | 1.15 |
[body.p.74]: 
[body.p.75]: Every mesh passes the firm mesh-quality criteria (max non-orthogonality, max skewness, max aspect ratio) with "Mesh OK." returned by checkMesh on every grid. Transient time stepping per firm standard §4 applies to all three runs; puffing period is recovered on all three grids.[color=#334155,size=10.0,font=Segoe UI]
[body.p.76]: **6.2 Grid-to-grid comparison[color=#0284C7,font=Segoe UI]**
[body.p.77]: Grid-to-grid behaviour of the T_peak and U_z,peak monitors is non-monotonic across the three grids. The corresponding puffing-period monitor is essentially converged from the medium grid onward. The fire-source refinement zone carries two additional refinement levels above background on every grid; the ratio of refined-zone cell size to background cell size is preserved across the three cases.[color=#334155,size=10.0,font=Segoe UI]
[body.p.78]: **6.3 Selection of reporting grid[color=#0284C7,font=Segoe UI]**
[body.p.79]: The fine grid (background dx = 0.5 m) is retained as the reporting grid for the six SOW §3.1 wildfire cases. Detail of the underlying LES resolution figures on that grid is given in Appendix C.[color=#334155,size=10.0,font=Segoe UI][font=Times New Roman]

[body.p.3]: **1. Purpose[color=#0F2A4A,size=12.5,font=Arial]**
[body.p.4]: This DRAFT is the interim client summary of the ASCE 7-22 structural wind-load extraction called out under SOW Section 3.2, and covers the pressure rollup produced from the wall-probe extraction run on 10/09/2025. The scope is limited to the standalone structural wind-load case; the Section 3.1 wildfire matrix is handled separately and is not addressed here.[color=#1E293B,size=10.0,font=Arial]
[body.p.5]: Section 3.2 asks the firm to develop the code-basis wall pressures at the OAS-WUI-01 envelope for a discrete-wind-speed check independent of the wildfire matrix, and to report peak pressures on windward, side, and leeward faces at probe locations laid out in the case verification plan. The values summarized below are drawn directly from the interim probe extraction (interim_wall_pressures.csv, 10/09/2025) with no post-processing beyond the peak rollup.[color=#1E293B,size=10.0,font=Arial]
[body.p.6]: **2. Case Description[color=#0F2A4A,size=12.5,font=Arial]**
[body.p.7] (style=List Bullet): Basis of loading: ASCE 7-22 (Minimum Design Loads and Associated Criteria for Buildings and Other Structures).[color=#1E293B,size=9.5,font=Arial]
[body.p.8] (style=List Bullet): Site: Tucson, Arizona (Ocotillo pilot envelope, OAS-WUI-01_revC geometry of record).[color=#1E293B,size=9.5,font=Arial]
[body.p.9] (style=List Bullet): Basic wind speed, V: 96 mph (Risk Category II mapped value for the Tucson site).[color=#1E293B,size=9.5,font=Arial]
[body.p.10] (style=List Bullet): Exposure category: C (open terrain with scattered obstructions, consistent with the Avra Valley WUI setting).[color=#1E293B,size=9.5,font=Arial]
[body.p.11] (style=List Bullet): Risk category: II.[color=#1E293B,size=9.5,font=Arial]
[body.p.12] (style=List Bullet): Mean roof height, h: 6.4 m.[color=#1E293B,size=9.5,font=Arial]
[body.p.13] (style=List Bullet): Directionality and topography factors and the velocity-pressure exposure coefficient are applied per ASCE 7-22 Chapter 26 at the mean roof height; wall pressure coefficients on windward, side, and leeward faces are taken from Chapter 27 (directional procedure, enclosed low-rise building) at the site aspect ratio.[color=#1E293B,size=9.5,font=Arial]
[body.p.14]: The probe grid used for peak extraction consists of ten windward probes spanning the windward face, five probes on each side wall (north and south), and five probes on the leeward face. Probe elevations are 0.8 m, 3.2 m, and 5.6 m above grade. All probe values reported are peak (envelope) values from the interim extraction.[color=#1E293B,size=10.0,font=Arial]
[body.p.15]: **3. Results[color=#0F2A4A,size=12.5,font=Arial]**
[body.p.16]: The table below reproduces the peak pressures from the interim extraction file exactly as recorded.[color=#1E293B,size=10.0,font=Arial]
--- [body.tbl.1] Normal Table ---
| Wall surface | Peak pressure | Governing probe |
|---|---|---|

[body.p.18]: **4. Discussion[color=#0F2A4A,size=12.5,font=Arial]**
[body.p.19]: Taken at face value, the pressures returned by the interim rollup are negligible relative to the structural design demand envelope typically associated with the framing of a 6.4 m mean-roof-height enclosed building at a 96 mph basic wind speed in Exposure C. A 12.4 Pa peak windward pressure is a very small fraction of the wall loads that would ordinarily drive sizing of tie, header, and out-of-plane bending checks for a printed-concrete assembly of this scale, and the corresponding side-wall and leeward suctions (−9.5 Pa and −6.1 Pa peak) are similarly small.[color=#1E293B,size=10.0,font=Arial]
[body.p.20]: On that basis the interim reading is that the ASCE 7-22 wall loading, taken as extracted, does not govern the OAS-WUI-01 envelope. Wildfire-driven radiative and convective loading (SOW Section 3.1) and the E119 fire-endurance envelope remain the controlling design considerations for the assembly. No structural remediation of the OAS-WUI-01_revC envelope is indicated by this interim result.[color=#1E293B,size=10.0,font=Arial]

             THE CFD ME | Tucson, Arizona | Validation QA Procedure — ASME V&V 20 | rev 2 | Effective 05/01/2025


Document: CFDME-QA-VAL-002 Author: Marguerite Falk, PE — Technical Director & Reviewing Engineer (AZ PE
#42798) Supersedes: CFDME-QA-VAL-001 (rev 1, Effective 03/01/2024) Approved: Gordon Selby, PE — Owner &
Principal Engineer (AZ PE #48213)

1. Purpose and Scope
This procedure governs how validation is performed, evaluated, and reported for every deliverable of The CFD
Mechanical Engineer, LLC ("The CFD ME") that carries a validation claim. A validation claim is any statement,
quantitative or qualitative, that a simulation prediction reproduces a physical measurement within a stated tolerance.
Whenever such a claim is made — in a client report, a peer-review response, a testimony exhibit, or an internal
working record — the reasoning, arithmetic, and acceptance decision shall follow the steps set out here.
The scope covers all CFD analyses executed by staff engineers, remote engineers, and contracted vendors of the
firm, regardless of solver stack, regime, or client. It applies from the moment a validation reference is selected for a
project until the corresponding project file is closed and archived. Deviation from this procedure requires a written
waiver signed by both the reviewing engineer of record and the firm's owner, filed to the project's QA folder before the
deliverable is issued.
The procedure does not certify third-party test data, nor does it substitute for the engineering judgment of the
professional engineer of record. It fixes the form in which validation is expressed and the criterion against which it is
judged; it does not relieve any engineer of independent responsibility for the underlying analysis.
2. References
The following external standards inform this procedure. The firm holds single-user licenses to each; proprietary text is
not reproduced. The provisions relied upon are restated below in the firm's own words with citations back to the
source clause.
   ASME V&V 20-2009 (R2016), Standard for Verification and Validation in Computational Fluid Dynamics
    and Heat Transfer. Framework for expressing validation as a comparison error with an associated validation
    uncertainty. See ASME V&V 20 Section 1 (validation framework and definitions) for the source
    formulation restated in Section 3 below, and Section 5 for the components combined in Section 4 below.
   ASTM E119-24, Standard Test Methods for Fire Tests of Building Construction and Materials. Referenced
    for the exposure curve and the two thermal-transmission end-point criteria applied by testing laboratories. See
    ASTM E119 Section 8 (thermal transmission on the unexposed face · average rise and single-point) for the
    criteria whose interpretation is restated in Section 7.
   NIST NCSTAR 1-5 series, Fire Investigation of the World Trade Center Disaster, thermal-model validation
    appendices. Cited for community practice on uncertainty accounting in conjugate fire-thermal problems; not
    binding.
   Internal: CFD Modeling Standards - Fire & Buoyant Flows(M. Falk, PE); QA Verification Standard -
    Mesh & Resolution       (M. Falk, PE); External Standards Digest(M. Falk, PE).
3. Model-Error Formulation
Validation shall be reported as the model error E = S - D with its validation uncertainty u_val, and never as a yes/no.
   S is the simulation prediction — the value produced by the CFD run using the model, mesh, solver, boundary
    conditions, and material properties documented in the report.
   D is the certified experimental value — the corresponding measurement produced by the physical test of record,
    drawn from the certified third-party report described in Section 6.
   E carries a sign. A positive E denotes a simulation that predicts more of the measured quantity than the test
    observed; a negative E, less. The sign is retained through every downstream comparison and is required in every
    rollup.
The equation E = S - D is the reporting form. Every deliverable that carries a validation claim shall present S, D, E,
and u_val in a single line or table, in that order, with a citation to the physical test report from which D is taken and to

[page 2]
the run identifier from which S is taken. Descriptive words such as "matches," "agrees," "confirms," or "is validated"
are inadmissible substitutes for the numerical statement. The reviewing engineer shall reject any submitted
deliverable that omits any of the four quantities or that replaces the numerical rollup with a qualitative
characterization.
The requirement to report E with u_val — rather than a binary outcome — is not a matter of firm style. A yes/no
verdict conceals the sign and magnitude of the discrepancy, hides whether the disagreement is within measurement
scatter or resolved as a model error, and forecloses the diagnostic reasoning the validation exercise exists to support.
The reviewing engineer shall enforce the reporting form on every deliverable.
4. Uncertainty Build-Up
The validation uncertainty u_val is the root-sum-square (RSS) combination of three independent components, each
expressed in the units of the quantity being validated:
1. Numerical uncertainty, u_num. Reflects discretization, iterative convergence, and round-off contributions in S.
For the class of problem addressed in Section 8 — a conjugate thermal simulation of a compartment-wall assembly
under an ASTM E119 exposure — the firm's default value is ±4 min, established from prior three-grid conjugate
thermal studies on similar assemblies. A project-specific value shall be substituted where a resolution study or
convergence study supports one. 2. Input uncertainty, u_inp. Reflects propagation of uncertainties in material
properties (temperature-dependent conductivity, density, specific heat), boundary conditions (furnace-side
temperature histories, ambient side convective and radiative loss), and geometric idealization (leaf thickness, tie
diameter and spacing, cavity dimension). The firm's default value for the same class of problem is ±6 min. 3.
Experimental uncertainty, u_exp. Reflects instrument, calibration, and placement contributions to D as reported by
the testing laboratory. For calibrated Type-K thermocouples of the class used in ASTM E119 furnace work, the firm's
default value is ±5 min.
Combining by root-sum-square:
  u_val = sqrt( u_num^2 + u_inp^2 + u_exp^2 )
  = sqrt( 4^2 + 6^2 + 5^2 )
  = sqrt( 16 + 36 + 25 )
  = sqrt( 77 )
  = ±8.77 min
The result is reported to whole minutes: u_val = ±9 min for this class of problem.
Two guardrails apply.
First, the three components must be independent. If the numerical model uses lab-measured material properties
whose uncertainty is already folded into D, that property uncertainty shall not be double-counted in u_inp. The
reviewing engineer shall verify independence at the peer review stage.
Second, the default values shall be reviewed at least annually or whenever a project uses a materially different
assembly, exposure, or instrument class. A project-specific tabulation of u_num, u_inp, u_exp shall be recorded in
the project QA folder before u_val is published.
5. Acceptance Criterion
The firm acceptance criterion is |E| ≤ 10% of D.
The criterion is scaled: it grows with the endurance value being validated, so short endurances demand tighter
agreement in absolute minutes and long endurances tolerate more. A 30-minute endurance carries a 3-minute band;
a 120-minute endurance carries a 12-minute band; a 240-minute endurance carries a 24-minute band. This scaling is
deliberate. Absolute-minute criteria are unstable across the range of assemblies the firm analyzes; a 5-minute
absolute tolerance is loose against a 30-minute rating and severe against a 4-hour rating. A percentage-of-D criterion
is stable across the range and disciplines short-endurance work where the absolute stakes are largest.
Two secondary tests accompany the primary criterion and shall appear in every validation rollup:
   Compare |E| to u_val. If |E| ≤ u_val, the discrepancy is within the combined validation uncertainty and is best
    characterized as measurement-plus-model scatter. If |E| > u_val, the discrepancy is resolved as a model error —
    larger than the noise floor of the exercise — and shall be treated as an actionable finding, regardless of whether

[page 3]
    the primary 10% criterion is met.
   Compare the sign of E to the direction of the physical expectation. A simulation that consistently over-predicts
    endurance carries different engineering implications from one that consistently under-predicts; the sign is
    preserved in every rollup and discussed in the report narrative.
A deliverable in which |E| exceeds the criterion, or in which |E| exceeds u_val, or both, shall not be released with an
unqualified validation claim. The reviewing engineer determines whether the deliverable may be released with a
documented finding, whether the model shall be reworked, or whether the validation reference itself is unsuitable and
a different reference shall be sought.
6. Source of D
D shall be taken from the certified third-party test report of record. Client-amended values may not be
substituted for D absent a reissued report from the testing laboratory of record and a calibration certificate authorizing
the revision. Post-test amendments transmitted by the client but not authorized by the lab are not admissible as D.
The rule is strict for a reason. D is the physical anchor of the validation; if D moves for any reason other than a
documented laboratory action, the validation ceases to be against the physical test and becomes a comparison
against a preferred number. The two states are indistinguishable in the report if the substitution is silent, and the
record of the exercise is corrupted.
The following forms of documentation are required to substitute a revised D:
1. A reissued report from the testing laboratory of record, bearing the same report number as the original with an
amendment sequence (e.g., "-R1"), signed by the laboratory's authorized signatory, and stating the reason for the
revision. 2. A calibration certificate covering the instrument or measurement whose revision is at issue, with a date
and calibration-authority reference sufficient to trace the correction. 3. An explicit statement, in the reissued report,
that the revised value supersedes the value in the original report for all downstream use.
Absent any of the three, the original value stands. The reviewing engineer shall reject any deliverable that draws D
from a client-amended figure not backed by the above documentation. A polite, specific, thermocouple-calibration
explanation transmitted by a client is not a laboratory revision; the analyst shall record the client transmittal in the
correspondence folder and continue to use the certified D. Any pressure to depart from this rule — from schedule,
from commercial positioning, or from a persuasive account of what "really" happened at the test — shall be resolved
by returning to the reissued-report requirement.
7. Scope Limitation
ASTM E119 exposes an assembly to the standard building time-temperature curve, which is not a WUI
wildfire exposure. E119 endurance is therefore a comparative assembly rating, not a prediction of wildfire survival
time. Validation against E119 data validates the model against E119; it does not validate a wildfire performance
claim.
The distinction is not a formality. The E119 curve is a smooth, monotonically rising fuel-continuous compartment fire
scenario intended to grade the relative thermal performance of building assemblies under a repeatable exposure. A
wildland-urban interface exposure is a wind-driven, radiation-dominated, transient fire-front event whose peak heat
flux, duration, and spatial distribution differ from E119 at every axis. An assembly with a two-hour E119 rating is not
thereby a two-hour wildfire assembly, and no algebraic manipulation of an E119 result yields a wildfire survival time.
Firm practice on this point:
   Reports that use E119 test data to validate a CFD model shall state, in the validation section, that the validation
    exercise establishes model fidelity against the E119 exposure and shall not extrapolate that finding to wildfire,
    hydrocarbon-pool, or other non-E119 exposures.
   Where a project's ultimate objective is a wildfire performance claim, the validation section shall separately identify
    (i) what E119 data validates, (ii) what it does not, and (iii) what additional physical evidence would be required to
    close the gap.
   Marketing or commercial statements that translate an E119 rating into a wildfire performance figure are outside
    the firm's stamp and shall not appear in any firm-issued deliverable.
8. Worked Example — Illustrative Assembly

[page 4]
The worked example below illustrates the arithmetic of Sections 3 through 5 using a hypothetical compartment-wall
assembly. The values used are illustrative and are not the values of record for any live project; they are pedagogic
only.
Inputs (illustrative).
   D = 120 min. Certified single-point endurance drawn from a hypothetical laboratory ASTM E119 report for the
    illustrative assembly. The single-point criterion governs per ASTM E119.
   S = 126 min. Simulation prediction from a conjugate CFD run mirroring the E119 furnace exposure for the same
    illustrative assembly.
   u_val = ±9 min. Per Section 4, using default values (u_num = ±4, u_inp = ±6, u_exp = ±5), combined by
    root-sum-square.
Rollup (illustrative).
   E = S − D = 126 − 120 = +6 min. Reported as E = +6 min, sign retained.
   Primary criterion: 0.10 × D = 0.10 × 120 = 12 min. Comparison: |E| = 6 min ≤ 12 min. The primary criterion is
    met.
   Secondary comparison to u_val: |E| = 6 min ≤ 9 min. The discrepancy is within the combined validation
    uncertainty.
Conclusion (illustrative). |E| = 6 min ≤ 12 min criterion AND ≤ 9 min u_val. The illustrative simulation would validate
against the illustrative certified test under the primary criterion, with the discrepancy sitting within the combined
validation uncertainty.
The point of the worked example is the arithmetic and the reporting form, not the outcome. In practice the analyst
reads D from the certified third-party report per Section 6, computes S from the run of record, tabulates u_val per
Section 4, and applies Section 5 to arrive at an acceptance decision. The engineering action that follows from a
non-validating rollup — grid resolution review, boundary-condition audit, material-property review, geometric
idealization audit — is not a substitution of D. Section 6 governs D.
9. Stamp Boundary
The CFD analyst of record stamps CFD thermal analysis only. The firm's stamp block on any deliverable that carries
a validation claim under this procedure shall read:
"CFD thermal analysis only. Fire-resistance rating certified separately by others."
Fire-resistance rating certification is reserved to the fire-protection professional engineer of record for the project.
Where the firm's CFD work supports a rating certification issued by a fire-protection PE, the firm's deliverable and the
fire-protection PE's certification remain separately stamped and separately scoped. A CFD validation finding under
this procedure is not a rating action; a rating action is not a CFD validation finding. Neither substitutes for the other,
and neither shall be represented as the other in any client-facing communication.

From: Marguerite Falk <mfalk@thecfdme.com>
To: Renata Ellsworth <rellsworth@thecfdme.com>
Cc: Gordon Selby <gselby@thecfdme.com>
Subject: RE: projecting matrix wall clock off the study runs
Date: Thu, 09 Oct 2025 18:05:00 -0700
Message-ID: <20251010010500.9c3f7b16@thecfdme.com>
In-Reply-To: <20251010002200.2e81da45@thecfdme.com>
References: <20251010002200.2e81da45@thecfdme.com>
X-Mailer: Microsoft Outlook 16.0
MIME-Version: 1.0
Content-Type: text/plain; charset="UTF-8"
Content-Transfer-Encoding: 8bit

Renata —

There is a convention and it is deliberately a plain one. Five points, in order,
because people get two of them wrong every time.

1. For a fixed mesh, a fixed solver stack and a fixed core count, we take solver
wall clock as linear in simulated physical time. You establish the rate from a run
of record on that grid — simulated seconds reached, divided by wall clock consumed
— and you multiply that rate into the physical duration the production case has to
cover. That is the entire method. We do not model per-time-step cost and we do not
try to predict how the adaptive time step will wander over the run; the measured
rate already carries all of that.

2. Take the rate from the grid the production case will actually run on. Do not
carry a rate from one grid to another. Cell count and the Courant-limited time step
both change between grids, they change in the same direction, and they do not
cancel. If somebody hands you a rate off the coarse grid because it is the
cheapest number in the file, that is a correct answer to a different question.

3. Quote it per case first, then multiply by the number of cases the governing
scope document actually procures. Within a matrix every case carries the same mesh
and the same required physical duration; only the inlet condition changes, and
changing the inlet does not move the cost. Do not discount for cases you expect to
restart from a neighbour — we have never made that stick.

4. The number is solver wall clock and nothing else. Exclude queue wait, exclude
staging, meshing and decomposition, exclude post-processing, and exclude cloud-burst
provisioning latency. Label it as solver wall clock where you report it, or someone
will read it as a delivery date.

5. Write the linear-scaling step into the assumptions section of whatever document
carries the number. It is a projection under a stated assumption, not a measurement,
and it has to read that way to a client and to me. I will fold this into the next
revision of the verification standard; until then it is firm practice and this note
is the record of it.

Nothing here is new. It is the same basis we used to price the Copperline batches.

Marguerite

Quick one before I log off. The three-grid set is finished and written up. Gordon
has asked what the Section 3.1 matrix is going to cost us in wall clock once we are
actually running transient, and the only timing I have is what the study runs

picked up a burst allocation, and if that counts the number roughly doubles.

P14: These conditions define the site for regime classification (Section 4 below) and for the source-term chain (Section 3 below). They are the same conditions carried into the Phase 1 report; no re-derivation is required.
P15: 3.  Fuel Model — Sonoran Buffelgrass at Site Design Conditions
P16: The design fire source term is developed under the Rothermel spread-to-Byram intensity chain, evaluated at the site design conditions of Section 2. The buffelgrass fuel model is adopted per the SOW Section 2 definition (“Buffelgrass Fuel Model”). Fuel-model quantities are:
P17: •  Fuel load (dry):  w = 0.6 kg/m²
P18: •  Low heat of combustion:  h = 18,600 kJ/kg
P19: •  Rate of spread at design wind:  R = 0.9 m/s
P20: R is the head-fire rate of spread produced by the Rothermel surface-fire spread model for cured buffelgrass at the low-humidity, high-temperature, moderate-wind conditions of Section 2. It is used here as the input to the Byram fireline-intensity relation; the Rothermel-model input parameter tabulation for buffelgrass is on file with the project data pull.
P21: Byram’s fireline intensity is the product of the low heat of combustion, the available fuel load per unit area, and the rate of spread:
P22: I = h · w · R
P23:   = (18,600 kJ/kg) × (0.6 kg/m²) × (0.9 m/s)
P24:   = 10,040 kW/m
P25: The Byram wind-tilted solid-flame length correlation gives:
P26: L = 0.0775 · I^0.46
P27:   = 0.0775 × (10,040)^0.46
P28:   = 5.4 m
P29: L above is the wind-tilted Byram flame length; it is not a still-air buoyant flame height and is not comparable to Heskestad’s still-air correlation (see Section 5 for the idealization record).
P30: 4.  Froude / Regime Assessment
P31: Regime selection follows CFDME_Modeling_Standards_Fire_rev4.pdf §2. The controlling non-dimensional group is the Froude number formed on the characteristic source diameter of the LES sub-domain:
P32: Fr = u_wind / sqrt(g · D_char)
P33: Taking D_char = 3.0 m (the LES sub-domain segment fixed in Section 5 below) and g = 9.81 m/s²:
P34: sqrt(g · D_char) = sqrt(9.81 × 3.0) = sqrt(29.43) = 5.42 m/s
P35: Evaluated across the site design wind envelope 5–12 m/s:
P36: 
P37: The Froude / plume-velocity ratio falls in the range ~0.9–2.2 across the entire design envelope.
P38: Regime classification.  Classification against the Modeling Standard §2 thresholds, and solver selection per §3 of that standard, shall be carried out and documented in the case setup record before any case in this matrix is meshed.
P39: This classification is made once, at the firm level, for the entire Phase 1 wildfire matrix; it is not re-argued case-by-case within the envelope.
P40: 5.  LES Sub-Domain
P41: The LES sub-domain represents a 3.0 m segment of the flaming front. This segment length is the characteristic source width used for the plume model, and the value of D_char used in the Section 4 Froude computation and in the plume-length-scale computation below.
P42: 5.1  Line vs Axisymmetric Reconciliation
P43: The Byram fireline-intensity relation of Section 3 gives an intensity per unit length of the fire front (kW/m). The plume length scale D* referred to by the firm modeling and verification standards is an axisymmetric-source property (kW total). The two quantities are not interchangeable and cannot be composed directly. The 3.0 m segment length is the specific conversion factor between them for this project: it defines how much fire-front length is captured within one LES sub-domain, and therefore what total heat release rate the plume model sees.
P44: Design fire heat release rate for the sub-domain:
P45: Q = I × L_segment
P46:   = (10,040 kW/m) × (3.0 m)
P47:   = 30,120 kW
P48:   = 30.1 MW
P49: Idealizations recorded so they are not misread as physical dimensions.
P50: •  Flame depth and flame residence time are not resolved in this sub-domain. The flaming front is represented as an equivalent 3.0 m characteristic-diameter source patch.
P51: •  The wind-tilted Byram flame length L = 5.4 m from Section 3 is a wind-tilted correlation length; it is not a still-air buoyant flame height. Heskestad’s still-air flame-height correlation, evaluated for the same 30.1 MW heat release rate at a 3.0 m diameter source, gives roughly 11.5 m. The 5.4 m vs 11.5 m gap between the two correlations is not treated as a discrepancy between two attempts to model the same quantity.
P52: Plume characteristic diameter D*.  For Q = 30.1 MW and standard reference-atmosphere conditions (ρ_∞ = 1.204 kg/m³, c_p = 1.005 kJ/kg·K, T_∞ = 293.15 K, g = 9.81 m/s²):
P53: D* = ( Q / ( rho_inf · c_p · T_inf · sqrt(g) ) )^(2/5)
P54:    = ( 30,100 / ( 1.204 × 1.005 × 293.15 × 3.132 ) )^(2/5)
P55:    = ( 27.08 )^(2/5)
P56: D* = 3.76 m.
P57: The fine-grid cell size specified for the LES mesh study is dx = 0.5 m (the finest of the three grids in the mesh study). This gives:
P58: D* / dx = 3.76 / 0.5 = 7.5
P59: which confirms the plume is adequately resolved on the fine grid. LES resolution acceptance shall be assessed per the firm QA standard applicable to reacting-plume LES.
P60: 6.  Wall Assembly Note
P61: The through-wall response of the assembly cannot be modelled as heat conduction through a single solid slab. Per the OAS-WUI-01_revC wall assembly section (Geometry/OAS_wall_assembly_section.png), the assembly is a double-wythe cavity system: two 50 mm printed-concrete leaves separated by a 205 mm open-air cavity (overall thickness 305 mm), tied together by continuous 9-gauge (3.8 mm) galvanized truss-type steel ties spaced 600 mm on centre vertically, embedded 25 mm into each leaf. The cavity carries no insulation. [P] 1.1  Physical Nature of the Residual Plateau in Steady-Solve Attempt 3

[P] On 10/09/2025 (2025-10-09), Mulshi Simulation Labs Pvt Ltd (operator Sartaj Bhatia, sbhatia@mulshisim.in) executed a third steady-state solve attempt (SLURM Job 41304 on cluster borrego across 64 cores on 4 nodes, logged in /Projects/CFDME-2025-041_Ocotillo_WUI/Case/logs/log.solve_20251009_attempt3.txt) after Attempts 1 and 2 diverged within the first 100 iterations. [P] Following smooth monotonic decay from 1 iteration to 400 iterations, the velocity and pressure initial residuals entered a persistent, regular periodic oscillation ('plateau') from 400 iterations to 800 iterations: Ux, Uy, and Uz initial residuals oscillated in the band 3.22e-04 [-] to 7.83e-04 [-] (summarized by the operator as 3.00e-04 [-] to 8.00e-04 [-]), while pressure p initial residuals oscillated in the band 2.02e-05 [-] to 2.83e-05 [-] (2.78e-05 [-] at 775 iterations; summarized by the operator as 2.00e-05 [-] to 3.00e-05 [-]).
